get_current_position.description: Get where a satellite is at this moment, the point on Earth it is over, how high it is, and where to look for it from your location: the compass bearing, the angle above the horizon, and whether it is above the horizon at all.
get_current_position.name: get_current_position

parameters.description: The satellite's NORAD catalog number. Defaults to 25544, the International Space Station. To find another object's number, search for it at https://www.n2yo.com and read the NORAD ID off its page. Use the catalog number (100057), not the Alpha-5 form a TLE shows (A0057).
parameters.name: satellite_id

parameters.description: Latitude of the place you are observing from, in decimal degrees (-90 to 90). Negative is south of the equator.
parameters.name: latitude

parameters.description: Longitude of the place you are observing from, in decimal degrees (-180 to 180). Negative is west of Greenwich.
parameters.name: longitude

parameters.description: Height above sea level of the place you are observing from, in metres. Leave at 0 unless you are somewhere high; it barely moves the answer at everyday elevations.
parameters.name: observer_altitude

parameters.description: Optional. A time-zone database name such as 'America/New_York'. Every time in the result is also reported as local wall-clock time in this zone, which is what a person reading 'the ISS passes over at...' needs. Leave empty to get UTC only.
parameters.name: timezone

altitude_km.description: Height of the satellite above the ground, in kilometres.

azimuth.description: Compass bearing to look along from the observer, in degrees clockwise from north.

azimuth_compass.description: The same bearing as a compass point, e.g. 'WNW'. Worked out from the azimuth.

declination.description: Declination of the satellite on the sky, in degrees.

elevation.description: How high above the horizon to look, in degrees. 0 is the horizon, 90 is straight up; a negative value means the satellite is below the horizon.

is_above_horizon.description: Whether the satellite is above the observer's horizon at this moment, i.e. whether the elevation is positive.

latitude.description: Latitude of the point on the ground directly below the satellite, in degrees.

local_time.description: The same instant as wall-clock time in the requested time zone, or empty when no time zone was given.

longitude.description: Longitude of the point on the ground directly below the satellite, in degrees.

right_ascension.description: Right ascension of the satellite on the sky, in degrees.

satellite_id.description: NORAD catalog number of the satellite the answer is about.

time.description: The same instant as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time.

timestamp.description: The instant this position is for, in Unix seconds.

transactions_used.description: How many calls this API key has made in the last 60 minutes, as N2YO counts them. The free hourly limits are 1000 each for orbital elements and positions, and 100 each for visual passes, radio passes and 'what is above me'.

get_next_pass.description: Answer 'when can I next see it?' in one step: the soonest pass over your location, with how long until it starts, where it rises, how high it climbs and where it sets. Choose whether that means a pass you can see or one you can work by radio. Returns 'found: false' when nothing qualifies in the window rather than failing the step.
get_next_pass.display_str_template: Get the next pass of satellite {0}.
get_next_pass.name: get_next_pass

get_satellites_above.description: List everything N2YO is tracking in a patch of sky above your location right now, with each object's name, catalog number, launch date, height and the point on Earth it is over. Narrow the search to a category (Starlink, amateur radio, weather, the ISS) and set how wide a patch of sky to sweep.
get_satellites_above.name: get_satellites_above

get_tle.description: Get a satellite's current two-line element set: the orbital data every tracking and prediction tool reads. Returns both lines separately and as the plain text block those tools expect. Reports 'found: false' when the catalog number has no current elements rather than failing the step.

get_visual_passes.description: Get the times a satellite will be visible to the naked eye from your location: when it appears, where to look, how high it climbs, how bright it gets and how long it stays visible. A visible pass needs the satellite in sunlight over a dark sky, so this list is far shorter than the times it simply flies over.

description: Track satellites with N2YO: where the International Space Station (or any of the 35,000 catalogued objects) is right now, when it will next be visible from your back garden, when it will be high enough to work by radio, what is passing overhead at this moment, and the orbital elements tracking software needs.
